beliefs.practice: Read the DocumentDB/MongoDB connection string and any LLM/API keys exclusively from environment variables (or a local .env loaded at runtime) and never commit secrets into source control or logs.
Create a single long-lived MongoClient per process and reuse it for all requests (do not open a new client per request); close it cleanly on shutdown.
Enable TLS/SSL for connections and verify server certificates (do not disable certificate validation) when connecting to the managed cluster.
Use sensible socket and server selection timeouts (e.g., serverSelectionTimeoutMS and socketTimeoutMS) and tune them for your environment so client calls fail fast on unreachable clusters.
Implement automatic retries with exponential backoff for transient errors (network timeouts, 429/RequestRateTooLarge) and ensure idempotency of retried operations.
Use bulkWrite or batched update operations to persist CLV scores for many customers at once rather than issuing many single-document writes.
When updating CLV on a customer document, use $set (and upsert when appropriate) instead of replacing the entire document to avoid accidental data loss.
Design the partition key so related customer data and writes for a single customer fall into the same logical partition (e.g., customer_id) to keep updates atomic and efficient.
Create a compound index on fields used together in aggregation (e.g., customer_id + order_date or customer_id + purchase_id) to accelerate grouping and chronological queries.
For arrays you query or aggregate over (line items, product_ids), create appropriate multikey indexes and avoid unbounded arrays in documents that would make indexes explode.
Only return the fields required for computation (projection) in aggregation pipelines to reduce RU consumption and network transfer.
Limit aggregation pipeline stages and use $match early (preferably on the partition key) to reduce scanned records and RU costs.

When using the cluster's vector search features, explicitly set and validate index parameters (vector dimension, metric—cosine/Euclidean, HNSW/IVF parameters) to match the embedding model used by the LLM.
Avoid storing very large documents (keep documents well under the provider's document size limit) and instead normalize or put large blobs in object storage and reference them.
Record model/LLM outputs and the LLM rationale in structured fields and an append-only audit or history subdocument rather than overwriting the sole source-of-truth field so you can trace changes.
Sanitize and validate any values produced by the LLM before writing them back to the database (type checks, ranges, allowed enums for CLV tier) to avoid corrupting customer documents.
Use explain() / server-side explain plans and monitor index usage to verify that aggregations use the intended indexes; evaluate RU consumption of sample aggregation workloads.
Provision enough throughput (RUs or the appropriate instance tier) for aggregation jobs and index builds; schedule heavy batch processing during off-peak hours to avoid throttling.
Build indexes during low-traffic windows or use online index build options when available, because index creation can greatly increase RU consumption and impact latency.
Enable and configure backups and point-in-time restore where available so you can recover from accidental writes by the agent or faulty aggregation runs.

Use application-level or database-supported tracing/metrics (Azure Monitor, metrics for RU usage, request charge) and log slow aggregation/queries and throttling (HTTP 429s) for operational visibility.

Avoid multi-document transactions spanning partitions for CLV writes; prefer single-partition updates or design for per-customer partitioning—if multi-document transactions are needed, validate whether the MongoDB API on this cluster supports them before relying on them.
